Preface
Welcome to Principles of Macroeconomics: An Institutional and Social Science Perspective.
This textbook offers an analytical, empirical approach to macroeconomic systems, national accounting, business cycles, monetary mechanisms, and fiscal policy. It is structured around the analytical depth of Paul Krugman and Robin Wells (Macroeconomics, 6th ed.) and UC Berkeley Econ 2.
Use the left sidebar navigation to explore individual chapters or press s to initiate full-text keyword searches across the entire volume.

title: 1  Chapter 1: First Principles of Economics & Macroeconomic Systems
text:
Conceptual Introduction
While microeconomics zooms in on how individual households, workers, and firms make decisions in specific markets, macroeconomics steps back to examine the behavior of the entire economy as an interconnected system. Macroeconomists study economy-wide phenomena: why total national output (Real GDP) grows over decades, why recessions occasionally trigger widespread unemployment, what causes sustained inflation, and how central banks and governments use monetary and fiscal policies to stabilize economic fluctuations.
A foundational insight of macroeconomics is that the whole is more than the simple sum of its parts. In an economy where people and businesses buy from and sell to one another, one person’s spending is another person’s income. When many households or businesses change their behavior at the same time, feedback can produce aggregate outcomes different from what any individual intended—a possibility economists call the fallacy of composition.
The Paradox of Thrift is one possible short-run feedback mechanism. For an individual household facing financial uncertainty, cutting consumption and saving more may be prudent. If many households do this together, however, business sales can fall, reducing production, hiring, and household income. In a model with spare capacity, slow price adjustment, and no offsetting increase in investment or public spending, aggregate income may fall enough that total saving does not rise as intended. This result depends on those assumptions; it is not a universal prediction for every economy or time horizon.


Visual Representation
Figure 1 summarizes this conditional short-run feedback loop: lower consumption can reduce business revenue and household income, reinforcing efforts to save.






NoteClear It Up: Fallacy of Composition in Macroeconomics



What is true for a single individual is not automatically true for the whole economy at once. If one fan stands up at a stadium concert, they get a better view; if everyone stands up simultaneously, nobody sees better and everyone’s legs get tired. Similarly, if every firm cuts wages simultaneously to boost profits, worker purchasing power falls and consumer demand for those firms’ products shrinks.





Figure 1. A possible short-run feedback in the Paradox of Thrift. The mechanism assumes spare capacity and no immediate offset from investment or policy; actual outcomes depend on economic conditions.




Real-World Application: The 2008–2009 Great Recession and Household Deleveraging
The Great Recession offers a case for distinguishing a model mechanism from a historical explanation. When households try to repair balance sheets by cutting consumption, the short-run model predicts weaker sales and income if other spending does not offset the decline. Jones, Midrigan, and Philippon (2022) evaluate the household-leverage explanation and find that credit shocks account for only a small fraction of the aggregate employment decline in 2008–2010, while slowing the recovery. The saving-spending mechanism is useful for organizing the question, but it does not by itself establish the cause or size of a historical downturn.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
For the worked model, assume a closed economy with no government or foreign trade, fixed prices, spare productive capacity, fixed planned investment, and a constant marginal propensity to consume. If consumption depends on autonomous spending \(C_0\) and a fraction \(c\) of income \(Y\), private saving is \(S=Y-C\):
\[
C = C_0 + cY, \qquad S = Y - (C_0 + cY) = -C_0 + (1 - c)Y
\]
In this model’s equilibrium, planned saving equals planned investment (\(S=I_p\)). The setup illustrates a short-run possibility rather than a universal response.
Worked Problem: Suppose a closed economy has planned business investment fixed at \(I_p = \$200\text{ billion}\), and households initially consume according to \(C = 100 + 0.75Y\) (so initial saving is \(S = -100 + 0.25Y\)).

Find initial equilibrium national income \(Y_1^*\) and confirm that equilibrium saving equals \(\$200\text{ billion}\).
Suppose consumer anxiety causes households to cut autonomous consumption by \(\$50\text{ billion}\) (trying to save \(\$50\text{ billion}\) more at every income level), so \(C_{\text{new}} = 50 + 0.75Y\) and \(S_{\text{new}} = -50 + 0.25Y\). Compute the new equilibrium income \(Y_2^*\) and new total saving \(S_2^*\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Solve for Initial Equilibrium Income (\(Y_1^*\)) Where \(S = I_p\):

\[
-100 + 0.25Y_1^* = 200 \implies 0.25Y_1^* = 300 \implies Y_1^* = \mathbf{\$1{,}200\text{ billion}}
\]
Check equilibrium saving: \(S_1^* = -100 + 0.25(1{,}200) = -100 + 300 = \mathbf{\$200\text{ billion}}\).

Solve for New Equilibrium Income (\(Y_2^*\)) After the Saving Surge: Set \(S_{\text{new}} = I_p\):

\[
-50 + 0.25Y_2^* = 200 \implies 0.25Y_2^* = 250 \implies Y_2^* = \mathbf{\$1{,}000\text{ billion}}
\]
Check new equilibrium saving at \(Y_2^* = \$1{,}000\):
\[
S_2^* = -50 + 0.25(1{,}000) = -50 + 250 = \mathbf{\$200\text{ billion}}
\]
Conclusion: Under the stated assumptions, the \(\$50\) billion reduction in autonomous consumption lowers equilibrium income by \(\$200\) billion (from \(\$1{,}200\) billion to \(\$1{,}000\) billion), while equilibrium saving remains \(\$200\) billion. This is the paradox-of-thrift result for this model.

section: 1.2 The Expanded Circular Flow, Leakages, and Injections
text:
1.2 The Expanded Circular Flow, Leakages, and Injections

Conceptual Introduction
To track how dollars circulate across an open economy, macroeconomists add three sectors to the household-firm circular flow: the financial sector, which connects savers and borrowers; government, which collects taxes and purchases goods and services; and the rest of the world, which buys exports and sells imports.
In this four-sector accounting framework, expenditure on domestically produced final goods and services (\(Y\)) equals four spending components:
\[
Y \equiv C + I + G + NX, \qquad \text{where } NX = X - M
\]
Here \(C\) is household consumption, \(I\) is private investment spending, \(G\) is government purchases of goods and services, and \(NX\) is net exports (exports \(X\) minus imports \(M\)).
Three flows are called leakages: private saving (\(S\)), net taxes (\(T\)), and imports (\(M\)). Three flows are called injections: investment (\(I\)), government purchases (\(G\)), and exports (\(X\)). In the accounting equilibrium represented here, total leakages equal total injections:
\[
S + T + M = I + G + X
\]


Visual Representation
Figure 2 maps the expanded four-sector circular flow, distinguishing leakage channels (\(S, T, M\)) from injection channels (\(I, G, X\)) by both label and line style.



Figure 2. The Four-Sector Macroeconomic Circular Flow. Dashed orange arrows show leakages (\(S+T+M\)); solid teal arrows show injections (\(I+G+X\)).




Real-World Application: U.S. Budget Deficits and Trade Balances
Rearranging the leakage-injection identity \(S + T + M = I + G + X\) yields the fundamental open-economy accounting relation:
\[
(S - I) + (T - G) = (X - M) = NX
\]
Here \((S-I)\) is the private sector’s net saving balance and \((T-G)\) is public saving (a government budget surplus if positive, or deficit if negative). If public saving and private net saving are both negative, the identity implies \(NX<0\). This is an accounting relationship, not proof that a budget deficit causes a trade deficit; the private, public, and foreign balances are jointly linked.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Balancing total leakages against total injections confirms the expenditure identity:
\[
S + T + M = I + G + X \iff Y = C + I + G + (X - M)
\]
Worked Problem: In a macroeconomic model of an open economy (in billions of dollars), household consumption is \(C = \$900\), private saving is \(S = \$250\), net taxes are \(T = \$350\), government purchases are \(G = \$400\), private investment is \(I = \$300\), exports are \(X = \$200\), and imports are \(M = \$300\).

Verify that total leakages equal total injections.
Compute national income (\(Y\)) using both the income-disposition identity (\(Y = C + S + T\)) and the aggregate expenditure identity (\(Y = C + I + G + NX\)).

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compare Total Leakages and Total Injections:

\[
\text{Total Leakages} = S + T + M = \$250 + \$350 + \$300 = \mathbf{\$900\text{ billion}}
\]
\[
\text{Total Injections} = I + G + X = \$300 + \$400 + \$200 = \mathbf{\$900\text{ billion}}
\]
Total leakages equal total injections (\(\$900\text{B} = \$900\text{B}\)).

Compute National Income (\(Y\)) via Both Identities:

\[
Y_{\text{income}} = C + S + T = \$900 + \$250 + \$350 = \mathbf{\$1{,}500\text{ billion}}
\]
\[
NX = X - M = \$200 - \$300 = -\$100\text{ billion}
\]
\[
Y_{\text{expenditure}} = C + I + G + NX = \$900 + \$300 + \$400 + (-\$100) = \mathbf{\$1{,}500\text{ billion}}
\]
Conclusion: Both accounting views yield the exact same national income of \(\$1{,}500\text{ billion}\).

text:
1.3 Business Cycles, Stabilization Policy, and Long-Run Growth

Conceptual Introduction
If you trace U.S. Real GDP over the past century, two distinct patterns jump off the page: a steady upward trend across decades, interrupted periodically by jagged waves of expansion and contraction. Macroeconomists divide their discipline around these two horizons:

The Business Cycle (Short-Run Fluctuations): Alternating periods of economic expansion (rising output and falling unemployment) and recession (a broad downturn in output, income, and employment). The turning point from expansion to recession is a peak, and the bottom turning point where recovery begins is a trough.
Long-Run Economic Growth: The sustained upward trend in an economy’s potential productive capacity over decades, which determines long-run living standards across generations.

To smooth out painful short-run business cycles without derailing long-run growth, policymakers deploy two stabilization toolkits: fiscal policy (changes in federal government spending and tax rates enacted by Congress and the President) and monetary policy (changes in interest rates and financial conditions implemented by the Federal Reserve).


Visual Representation
Figure 3 is a schematic—not a data series—showing output fluctuating around a rising long-run trend, with illustrative peaks, troughs, contractions, and recoveries.



Figure 3. Schematic Business Cycle. The solid orange line represents illustrative output fluctuations around a dashed long-run trend; it is not observed U.S. GDP data.




Real-World Application: NBER Business Cycle Dating
In the United States, the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) Business Cycle Dating Committee identifies peaks and troughs using a broad set of indicators. It emphasizes economy-wide measures and notes there is no fixed rule about which indicators receive weight; a recession is not determined solely by a two-quarter GDP rule (NBER, n.d.).


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
The percentage output gap measures how far actual Real GDP (\(Y\)) deviates from estimated Potential GDP (\(Y^*\)):
\[
\text{Output Gap } (\%) = \frac{Y - Y^*}{Y^*} \times 100\%
\]
Worked Problem: For an illustrative calculation, suppose estimated Potential Real GDP is \(Y^*=\$25.0\) trillion and actual Real GDP is \(Y=\$24.2\) trillion. Compute the dollar output gap and the percentage output gap. Potential GDP is estimated rather than directly observed.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute the Dollar Output Gap (\(Y - Y^*\)):

\[
Y - Y^* = \$24.2\text{ trillion} - \$25.0\text{ trillion} = \mathbf{-\$0.8\text{ trillion}\ (-\$800\text{ billion})}
\]

Compute the Percentage Output Gap:

\[
\text{Output Gap } (\%) = \frac{-0.8}{25.0} \times 100\% = -0.032 \times 100\% = \mathbf{-3.2\%}
\]
Conclusion: In this example, actual output is \(3.2\%\) below estimated potential output, a dollar gap of \(\$800\) billion.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Hodrick-Prescott Trend Decomposition



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: The Hodrick–Prescott filter decomposes observed log Real GDP \(y_t=\ln(Y_t)\) into a smooth trend \(\tau_t\) and a residual component \(c_t=y_t-\tau_t\) by solving:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\{\tau_t\}} \quad
&\sum_{t=1}^{T} (y_t - \tau_t)^2 \\
&+ \lambda \sum_{t=2}^{T-1}
\left[ (\tau_{t+1} - \tau_t) - (\tau_t - \tau_{t-1}) \right]^2
\end{aligned}
\]
For quarterly data, \(\lambda=1{,}600\) is a widely used convention (Hodrick and Prescott, 1997). The residual is not automatically stationary, and the filtered trend is not a direct observation of potential GDP.




Selected References

National Bureau of Economic Research. “Business Cycle Dating.” https://www.nber.org/research/business-cycle-dating
Jones, Callum, Virgiliu Midrigan, and Thomas Philippon. 2022. “Household Leverage and the Recession.” Econometrica 90(5): 2471–2505. NBER Working Paper 16965. https://www.nber.org/papers/w16965
Hodrick, Robert J., and Edward C. Prescott. 1997. “Postwar U.S. Business Cycles: An Empirical Investigation.” Journal of Money, Credit and Banking 29(1): 1–16. https://doi.org/10.2307/2953682

title: 2  Chapter 2: The Macroeconomic Production Possibilities Frontier & Capital Deepening
text:
Conceptual Introduction
Every nation faces an intertemporal macroeconomic trade-off between living well today and producing more tomorrow. To visualize this choice, macroeconomists place Consumer Goods (\(C\))—such as food, clothing, streaming entertainment, and restaurant meals that provide immediate satisfaction—on one axis of the Macroeconomic Production Possibilities Frontier, and Capital Goods (\(K\))—such as factories, power grids, cargo ships, semiconductor equipment, and research laboratories—on the other axis.
Because capital goods are durable inputs used to produce future goods and services, a nation’s operating point along its current PPF affects its capacity for long-run secular growth:

High-Consumption Strategy: Devoting nearly all resources to immediate consumer goods raises current living standards today, but leaves little net investment to replace worn-out machinery (depreciation)—causing the future PPF to stagnate or grow slowly.
High-Investment Strategy (Capital Deepening): Sacrificing some current consumption to build physical capital and infrastructure increases the economy’s capital-to-labor ratio (\(\Delta K > 0\)), shifting Potential GDP (\(Y^*\)) and the entire PPF outward in future years.

Real-World Connection. A data-center or power-grid project uses construction labor, equipment, and materials that could have gone to other production today. Whether the investment raises future productive capacity depends on the services the completed capital provides and whether gross investment exceeds depreciation.


Visual Representation
Figure 1 contrasts two nations starting on identical frontiers in 2026: Country A prioritizes current consumption (\(C_A\)), while Country B invests heavily in capital goods (\(K_B\)), achieving a substantially larger frontier by 2036.



Figure 1. Capital Deepening and Future PPF Expansion. Choosing point \(B\) (higher capital investment today) sacrifices current consumption relative to point \(A\), but accelerates capital accumulation and shifts the future frontier much further outward.




Mathematical Foundation
Next year’s physical capital stock (\(K_{t+1}\)) equals this year’s capital stock (\(K_t\)) plus gross investment (\(I_t\)) minus capital depreciation (\(\delta K_t\), where \(\delta\) is the annual depreciation rate):
\[
K_{t+1} = K_t + I_t - \delta K_t, \qquad \text{Net Investment} = I_t - \delta K_t
\]
Worked Problem: An economy begins Year 1 with a physical capital stock of \(K_1 = \$10{,}000\text{ billion}\). Each year, \(6\%\) of existing capital wears out (\(\delta = 0.06\)).

Compute annual capital depreciation in Year 1.
Calculate Year 2 capital stock (\(K_2\)) and net capital deepening (\(\Delta K\)) if gross investment is \(I_1 = \$950\text{ billion}\).
Determine the minimum gross investment required just to keep the capital stock from shrinking.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute Annual Depreciation (\(\delta K_1\)):

\[
\text{Depreciation} = 0.06 \times \$10{,}000\text{ billion} = \mathbf{\$600\text{ billion}}
\]

Compute Net Investment (\(\Delta K\)) and Year 2 Capital Stock (\(K_2\)):

\[
\Delta K = I_1 - \delta K_1 = \$950\text{ billion} - \$600\text{ billion} = \mathbf{+\$350\text{ billion}}
\]
\[
K_2 = \$10{,}000\text{ billion} + \$350\text{ billion} = \mathbf{\$10{,}350\text{ billion}}
\]

Identify Break-Even Maintenance Investment: To keep \(\Delta K = 0\), gross investment must at least replace worn-out capital: \(I_{\min} = \delta K_1 = \mathbf{\$600\text{ billion}}\).

Conclusion: Investing \(\$950\text{ billion}\) covers \(\$600\text{ billion}\) in depreciation and adds \(+\$350\text{ billion}\) in net capital deepening, shifting the economy’s future PPF outward.

text:
2.2 Output Gaps vs. Secular Growth on the Macro PPF

Conceptual Introduction
A common source of confusion in public policy debates is mixing up short-run cyclical recovery with long-run structural growth. On the Macroeconomic PPF, these two processes look completely different:

Recessionary Gap and Cyclical Recovery (Movement Inside to On the Frontier): During a recession, laid-off workers and idle factories push the economy to an interior point inside its existing PPF (\(Y < Y^*\)). Economic recovery—aided by countercyclical monetary or fiscal stimulus—puts idle resources back to work and moves the economy back out to its existing frontier, without changing Potential GDP (\(Y^*\)).
Overheating / Inflationary Gap (Unsustainable Temporary Push): Actual GDP can temporarily exceed an estimate of potential GDP (\(Y > Y^*\)) when labor and equipment are used unusually intensively, putting upward pressure on inflation. This does not represent a sustainable point beyond the PPF; potential GDP is an estimate of normal sustainable output, not a directly observed frontier.
Secular Growth (Outward Shift of the Frontier Itself): Expanding long-run Potential GDP (\(Y^*\)) requires expanding the PPF boundary itself through capital accumulation, labor-force growth, human capital, and technological progress.

Real-World Connection. Growth accounting, associated with Robert Solow, separates output growth explained by measured changes in capital and labor from a residual associated with productivity. The residual is not a direct measure of one particular technology; it also reflects influences not captured by measured inputs.


Visual Representation
Figure 2 distinguishes a cyclical recovery from an interior recession point (\(R \to E_1\) along an unchanged frontier) from true secular economic growth (\(E_1 \to E_2\) onto an expanded frontier).






NoteClear It Up: Demand Stimulus Restores Capacity; Supply Drivers Expand It



Lowering interest rates or cutting taxes during a recession helps close a negative output gap by moving the economy from an idle interior point (\(R\)) back to its current PPF (\(E_1\)). However, once the economy reaches full employment on the frontier, demand stimulus alone cannot push the PPF outward—long-run living standards depend on productivity, education, and investment!





Figure 2. Cyclical Recovery vs. Secular Growth. Moving from \(R\) to \(E_1\) eliminates recessionary unemployment by restoring full utilization of existing capacity. Moving from \(E_1\) to \(E_2\) represents long-run secular growth via outward expansion of the PPF.




Mathematical Foundation
Aggregate production links Potential Output (\(Y^*\)) to Total Factor Productivity (\(A\)), physical capital (\(K\)), and full-employment labor (\(L^*\)):
\[
Y^* = A \cdot f(K, L^*)
\]
Using the Rule of 70, the approximate number of years required for Real GDP per capita to double at an annual growth rate of \(g\%\) is:
\[
\text{Doubling Time (Years)} \approx \frac{70}{g}
\]
In this approximation, enter \(g\) as a percentage value (for example, \(2.0\), not \(0.02\)). For an exact annual-compounding calculation, use \(Y_n=Y_0(1+r)^n\), where \(r\) is the annual growth rate written as a decimal.
Worked Problem: Assume each country’s annual growth rate remains constant and income compounds once per year. Country X grows at \(r_X=0.02\), whereas Country Y grows at \(r_Y=0.035\). Both start with Real GDP per capita of \(\$20{,}000\) in 2026.

Use the Rule of 70 to compute how many years it takes each country to double its living standard to \(\$40{,}000\).
Use annual compounding to compute each country’s Real GDP per capita after \(70\) years (in 2096).

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Apply the Rule of 70:

\[
\text{Country X Doubling Time} = \frac{70}{2.0} = \mathbf{35\text{ years}}
\]
\[
\text{Country Y Doubling Time} = \frac{70}{3.5} = \mathbf{20\text{ years}}
\]

Compute Real GDP per Capita After \(70\) Years:

\[
Y_{70,X} = \$20{,}000(1+0.02)^{70} \approx \mathbf{\$79{,}991}
\]
\[
Y_{70,Y} = \$20{,}000(1+0.035)^{70} \approx \mathbf{\$222{,}257}
\]
Conclusion: Under these assumptions, Country Y’s income per person after 70 years is about \(2.8\) times Country X’s. The Rule of 70 gives useful approximate doubling times; the compound-growth formula supplies the 70-year values.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Solow Growth Accounting Equation



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Assuming a Cobb-Douglas aggregate production function \(Y = A K^\alpha L^{1-\alpha}\) with capital share \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\), taking natural logarithms and differentiating with respect to time decomposes output growth into three measurable sources:
\[
\frac{\Delta Y}{Y} \approx \frac{\Delta A}{A} + \alpha \frac{\Delta K}{K} + (1 - \alpha)\frac{\Delta L}{L}
\]
Here \(\frac{\Delta A}{A}\) is Total Factor Productivity (TFP) growth—the portion of output growth not explained by measured increases in capital or labor hours.

crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply and Demand: Macroeconomic Foundations

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply and Demand: Macroeconomic Foundations
text:
Conceptual Introduction
In microeconomics, supply and demand explain how the price of a single product—such as coffee, avocados, or apartment rent—adjusts to balance buyers and sellers in that specific market. When the price of a hospital visit or a carton of eggs rises while most other prices remain stable, economists call that a change in a relative price. Relative price changes are vital market signals: they tell consumers to economize on scarcer goods and tell producers where to direct resources.
Macroeconomics, by contrast, focuses on the general price level—the overall average price of a broad basket of goods and services across the entire economy. A sustained, economy-wide upward climb in a broad price index is called inflation (while a sustained decline in the broad price level is deflation). A rise in the broad index means that a dollar buys less of its weighted basket on average; it does not require every category’s price to rise. A local drought that raises lettuce prices, for example, changes lettuce’s relative price even if the broad index is unchanged.


Visual Representation
Figure 1 compares the all-items CPI with its medical-care component at two observation dates. Both series are rebased to 100 in May 2015; the points show the two observations, not the intervening monthly path.






NoteClear It Up: A One-Time Price Spike Is Not Ongoing Inflation



If a temporary supply disruption pushes gasoline prices up by \(15\%\) in one month and prices then stay flat at that higher level, the price level is higher, but the inflation rate (the percentage rate of change from month to month) returns to zero! Inflation measures the speed at which the broad price level is rising over time.





Figure 1. Two-observation comparison using FRED monthly CPI data. Medical care rose less than the all-items index between May 2015 and October 2026, so its price fell relative to the all-items basket over that interval.




Real-World Application: FRED Medical Care (CPIMEDSL) vs. All-Items CPI (CPIAUCSL)
FRED’s seasonally adjusted CPIAUCSL (all items) was 237.001 in May 2015 and 337.476 in October 2026; CPIMEDSL (medical care) was 446.743 and 595.675 on those same dates. Each series uses 1982–1984 = 100. First calculate the growth in each index:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{All-items growth} &= \frac{337.476-237.001}{237.001}\times100\% = 42.39\%,\\
\text{Medical-care growth} &= \frac{595.675-446.743}{446.743}\times100\% = 33.34\%.
\end{aligned}
\]
To calculate the change in medical care’s price relative to the all-items basket, compare the component-to-all-items ratio at the two dates:
\[
\left(\frac{595.675/337.476}{446.743/237.001}-1\right)\times100\%=-6.36\%.
\]
Thus, medical care’s relative price fell by 6.36% over these observations even though both price indexes rose. The all-items CPI represents an average urban-consumer basket, not every household’s exact spending pattern.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
A price index compares the current dollar cost of a fixed market basket against its base-period cost, and the inflation rate (\(\pi_t\)) measures the percentage change in that index between periods \(t-1\) and \(t\):
\[
\text{Price Index}_t = \frac{\text{Cost of Basket}_t}{\text{Cost of Basket}_{\text{base}}} \times 100, \qquad \pi_t = \frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}} \times 100\%
\]
Worked Problem: Suppose a simplified urban household basket costs \(\$1{,}200\) in the base year (2024), rises to \(\$1{,}260\) in 2025, and reaches \(\$1{,}310.40\) in 2026. Compute the price index for 2024, 2025, and 2026, and calculate the annual inflation rate for 2025 and 2026.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute the Price Index for Each Year (Base Year 2024 = 100):

\[
P_{2024} = \frac{\$1{,}200}{\$1{,}200} \times 100 = \mathbf{100.0}
\]
\[
P_{2025} = \frac{\$1{,}260}{\$1{,}200} \times 100 = \mathbf{105.0}
\]
\[
P_{2026} = \frac{\$1{,}310.40}{\$1{,}200} \times 100 = \mathbf{109.2}
\]

Calculate Annual Inflation Rates (\(\pi_{2025}\) and \(\pi_{2026}\)):

\[
\pi_{2025} = \frac{105.0 - 100.0}{100.0} \times 100\% = \mathbf{5.0\%}
\]
\[
\pi_{2026} = \frac{109.2 - 105.0}{105.0} \times 100\% = \frac{4.2}{105.0} \times 100\% = \mathbf{4.0\%}
\]
Conclusion: Notice that while the price level continued rising in 2026 (from \(105.0\) to \(109.2\)), the inflation rate slowed from \(5.0\%\) to \(4.0\%\)—a process economists call disinflation (slower positive inflation, not falling prices).

section: 3.2 Nominal vs. Real Values and Purchasing Power
text:
3.2 Nominal vs. Real Values and Purchasing Power

Conceptual Introduction
Because inflation changes the measuring stick of money over time, comparing raw dollar figures across different decades is misleading. A \(\$50{,}000\) salary in 1990 bought far more housing, groceries, and tuition than a \(\$50{,}000\) salary buys today. To make valid comparisons across time, macroeconomists strictly separate nominal values (measured in current, unadjusted dollars of the period) from real values (adjusted for price-level changes to reflect true purchasing power in constant base-period dollars).
The same distinction governs wages and interest rates:

Real Wage: Measures how many goods and services a worker’s paycheck can actually purchase. If your nominal hourly wage rises by \(3\%\) while consumer prices rise by \(5\%\), your real wage falls by roughly \(2\%\).
Real Interest Rate (\(r\)): Measures the true purchasing-power return earned by savers or paid by borrowers after subtracting inflation (\(\pi\)) from the stated nominal interest rate (\(i\))—summarized by the Fisher Equation: \(r \approx i - \pi\).







NoteClear It Up: A Nominal Raise Can Be a Real Pay Cut



A larger paycheck in dollars does not guarantee more purchasing power. Compare the percentage change in nominal pay with the percentage change in the price index; if prices rise faster, the real wage falls.




Visual Representation
Figure 2 contrasts a rising nominal wage index against a flat or declining real wage index when price-level inflation outpaces paycheck growth.



Figure 2. Nominal Wages vs. Real Purchasing Power. Even when a worker’s nominal wage increases steadily over time, if the broad price level rises faster than nominal pay, the worker’s real purchasing power declines.




Real-World Application: Minimum Wage Purchasing Power Across Decades
For covered nonexempt employees, the U.S. federal minimum wage has been \(\$7.25\) per hour since July 24, 2009. If the nominal rate stays fixed while the CPI rises, its purchasing power falls. This illustrates why minimum-wage comparisons should distinguish the stated dollar amount from its real value.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
To convert any nominal dollar amount \(X_t^{\text{nominal}}\) into constant base-period purchasing power (\(X_t^{\text{real}}\)):
\[
X_t^{\text{real}} = X_t^{\text{nominal}} \times \frac{P_{\text{base}}}{P_t}, \qquad r \approx i - \pi
\]
Worked Problem: Suppose a paralegal’s nominal salary was \(\$52{,}000\) in May 2015 and \(\$68{,}000\) in October 2026. For these months, CPIAUCSL was \(P_{2015}=237.001\) and \(P_{2026}=337.476\).

Express the 2026 salary in constant 2015 dollars to determine whether the paralegal’s real purchasing power increased or decreased.
Calculate the percentage change in real salary between 2015 and 2026.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Deflate the 2026 Nominal Salary into 2015 Base Dollars:

\[
\text{Salary}_{2026}^{\text{real (May 2015 \$)}} = \$68{,}000 \times \frac{237.001}{337.476} \approx \mathbf{\$47{,}754.71}
\]

Compute the Percentage Change in Real Purchasing Power:

\[
\%\Delta \text{Real Salary} = \frac{\$47{,}754.71 - \$52{,}000}{\$52{,}000} \times 100\% = \frac{-\$4{,}245.29}{\$52{,}000} \times 100\% \approx \mathbf{-8.16\%}
\]
Conclusion: The hypothetical nominal salary rose by 30.77%, while CPIAUCSL rose by 42.39%. After adjusting for prices, purchasing power fell by 8.16%.

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply and Demand: Macroeconomic Foundations
section: 3.3 Market Clearing and Sticky Wages in a Labor Market
text:
3.3 Market Clearing and Sticky Wages in a Labor Market

Conceptual Introduction
In a labor market, firms demand labor and workers supply it. The wage coordinates their plans: at a wage where labor demanded equals labor supplied, the simple competitive model clears. In practice, nominal wages may adjust slowly because of contracts, pay-review schedules, or workplace policies.
If labor demand falls while the nominal wage is temporarily fixed above the new market-clearing wage, firms want fewer workers than households want to supply. In this simplified model, employment is limited by the short side of the market, so the gap is excess labor supply. It is an illustration of one possible adjustment mechanism, not a complete account of unemployment.
When wages are flexible in this model, the wage can move toward a new labor-market equilibrium. That result does not imply that all unemployment disappears in the real economy, nor does the labor-market diagram by itself determine potential GDP. Search frictions, skills, institutions, and the link from employment to output are outside this model; this section is not an aggregate-demand/aggregate-supply analysis.


Visual Representation
Figure 3 uses the labor-market quantities in the worked problem. Coordinates use \(x=L/40\) and \(y=W/10\) for legibility; labels give labor in millions and wage dollars per hour.



Figure 3. A leftward labor-demand shift lowers the model’s flexible-wage equilibrium from \((L,W)=(80,\$30)\) to \((60,\$20)\). If the wage stays at \(\$30\), labor demanded is 20 million while labor supplied is 80 million; the gap is excess labor supply in this stylized model.




Real-World Application: Downward Nominal Wage Rigidity
Federal Reserve research documents downward nominal wage rigidity, but also finds that some continuing workers receive nominal wage cuts. Wage freezes, pay cuts, reduced hiring, and layoffs are possible adjustment margins; this example isolates only the fixed-wage case and should not be read as a universal description of recession behavior.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
At a fixed nominal wage \(\bar{W}\), employment in the simplified labor-market model is limited by the short side:
\[
L_{\text{employed}} = \min\left(L_d(\bar{W}), \; L_s(\bar{W})\right)
\]
If labor supplied exceeds labor demanded, the difference is excess labor supply in this model; it is not automatically an official unemployment statistic.
Worked Problem: In a hypothetical labor market, labor demand is \(L_d = 200 - 4W\) and labor supply is \(L_s = 20 + 2W\), with quantities in millions of workers and \(W\) in dollars per hour. A recession shifts labor demand left to \(L_d^{\text{new}} = 140 - 4W\).

Compute employment and excess labor supply if the nominal wage remains fixed at \(\$30\).
Find the new flexible-wage equilibrium \((W_2^*, L_2^*)\) in this model.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Evaluate the Fixed-Wage Outcome at \(W=\$30\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
L_d^{\text{new}}(30) &= 140 - 4(30) = 140 - 120 = 20\text{ million},\\
L_s(30) &= 20 + 2(30) = 20 + 60 = 80\text{ million}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Employment is the smaller quantity, \(20\) million. Excess labor supply is \(80-20=\mathbf{60\text{ million}}\) in this hypothetical model.

Solve for the Flexible-Wage Equilibrium (\(L_d^{\text{new}} = L_s\)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
140 - 4W_2^* &= 20 + 2W_2^*\\
120 &= 6W_2^*\\
W_2^* &= \$20.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitute the wage into either schedule:
\[
L_2^* = 20 + 2(20) = \mathbf{60\text{ million}}.
\]
Conclusion: Employment is 20 million at the fixed wage and 60 million at the flexible-wage equilibrium in this simplified model. The 60-million gap is excess labor supply, not a measured unemployment count.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Exact vs. Approximate Fisher Equation



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: Using decimal rates, the Fisher relation is \(1+i=(1+r)(1+\pi)\). Solving for the exact real rate gives:
\[
r = \frac{i - \pi}{1 + \pi}
\]
For an expected real return, use expected inflation; realized inflation gives an ex-post real return. When inflation is small, \(r \approx i-\pi\) is a useful approximation.

section: Practice Questions
text:
Practice Questions

A price index rises from 100 to 105 in one year and then to 109.2 the next year. Which statement is correct?


Inflation is 5% in the first year and 4% in the second; this is disinflation. Correct: The second annual rate is lower but remains positive.
Inflation is 5% in both years. Incorrect: The second rate is \((109.2-105)/105 \times 100\%=4\%\).
Prices fell by 4% in the second year. Incorrect: The index rose from 105 to 109.2; inflation slowed but stayed positive.
The price level fell by 1%. Incorrect: This confuses the change in the inflation rate with the change in the price index.


From May 2015 to October 2026, CPIAUCSL rose from 237.001 to 337.476 while CPIMEDSL rose from 446.743 to 595.675. What happened to medical care’s price relative to the all-items basket?


It rose by 9.05 percentage points. Incorrect: This subtracts the two growth rates but does not calculate the change in the component-to-all-items price ratio.
It fell by about 6.36%. Correct: The ratio \((CPIMEDSL/CPIAUCSL)\) fell by this percentage between the observations.
It rose by 33.34%. Incorrect: That is medical care’s own index growth, not its relative-price change.
It did not change because both indexes increased. Incorrect: The indexes grew at different rates.


In the labor-market example, labor demand after a recession is \(L_d=140-4W\), supply is \(L_s=20+2W\), and the wage is fixed at \(\$30\). What does the model imply?


Employment is 80 million and excess labor supply is zero. Incorrect: It uses labor supplied as employment even though firms demand only 20 million workers.
Employment is 20 million and excess labor supply is 60 million. Correct: Demand is 20 million and supply is 80 million; employment is the short side.
Employment is 60 million and excess labor supply is 20 million. Incorrect: These values do not equal the model’s quantities at \(W=\$30\).
The model proves that measured unemployment is 60 million. Incorrect: It gives a hypothetical excess-supply gap, not an official unemployment statistic.

text: 4.1 Defining Gross Domestic Product and Avoiding Double Counting
crumbs: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP

title: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP
text:
Conceptual Introduction
To gauge the health and size of a national economy, macroeconomists rely on Gross Domestic Product (GDP)—defined strictly as the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s borders during a given time period. Every single word in that definition acts as an accounting rule:

Market Value: Physical quantities of apples, airplanes, and haircuts are converted into a common dollar metric using market prices (with imputed rental values included for owner-occupied homes).
Final Goods and Services Only: To prevent double counting, GDP counts only finished products sold to end users—or equivalently, sums each firm’s value added at every stage of production—excluding intermediate goods (such as microchips, flour, or sheet steel) used up to make final goods.
Produced Within Domestic Borders: GDP is geographic—a Toyota Camry assembled in Kentucky counts in U.S. GDP, whereas a Ford assembled in Mexico counts in Mexican GDP (contrasting with Gross National Product, which tracks ownership).
Current Production Only: GDP excludes sales of used cars, existing homes, pure financial transfers (buying stocks or bonds), and government transfer payments (Social Security checks), because no new current good or service was produced.

These rules make GDP a measure of current market production, not a balance sheet of national wealth or a complete measure of well-being. Unpaid household work and leisure are generally outside its market-production boundary. GDP totals also do not show how income is distributed, and they do not subtract every environmental or social cost associated with production. Those limits do not make GDP useless; they define the narrower question it answers.


Visual Representation
Figure 1 uses an illustrative three-stage supply chain—from silicon wafer to laptop processor to retail laptop—to show why summing each firm’s value added (\(\$100 + \$250 + \$650 = \$1{,}000\)) matches the final retail price without counting intermediate sales twice. The dollar amounts are hypothetical teaching values, not reported company data.



Figure 1. Value-Added Accounting Eliminates Double Counting. Summing gross receipts across all three firms (\(\$100 + \$350 + \$1{,}000 = \$1{,}450\)) would count intermediate components twice; summing each stage’s value added equals the final retail value of \(\$1{,}000\).


Cross-Country Real GDP, 1990–2024. The two panels compare each country’s real-GDP path and its annual growth rate. Each index starts at 100 in 1990; the first panel uses a logarithmic vertical scale so equal vertical distances represent equal percentage changes.



Figure 2. Real GDP in the United States, Japan, China, and the United Kingdom, 1990–2024. The upper panel indexes each country’s output to 100 in 1990; the lower panel reports annual percentage growth. Shaded windows mark the event periods keyed to notes 1–4 below.


How to read the panels. Let \(Y_{i,t}\) denote country \(i\)’s real GDP in year \(t\). The index is \(I_{i,t}=100 \times \frac{Y_{i,t}}{Y_{i,1990}}\), so an index of 150 means output is 50% above its 1990 level. Annual growth is \(g_{i,t}=\frac{Y_{i,t}-Y_{i,t-1}}{Y_{i,t-1}}\times100\%\), the percentage change from the previous year. The index normalizes countries’ starting levels; its logarithmic vertical scale makes equal distances represent equal proportional changes.
Selected event windows:

1. United States, 2007–2009: The NBER dates the recession from December 2007 to June 2009. World Bank real GDP growth was \(-2.6\%\) in 2009; the annual series shows the timing and scale of the downturn, not a causal estimate. https://www.nber.org/research/data/us-business-cycle-expansions-and-contractions
2. Japan, 2011: Real GDP growth was \(-0.2\%\). The IMF’s contemporaneous assessment said the Great East Japan earthquake halted the nascent recovery and that supply disruptions remained a risk. https://www.imf.org/en/news/articles/2015/09/28/04/52/mcs060711
3. United Kingdom, 2016–2019: Annual growth remained positive (\(2.2\%\) in 2016, \(3.0\%\) in 2017, \(1.6\%\) in 2018, and \(1.3\%\) in 2019). The OBR reported slower growth after the referendum and weaker investment, while cautioning that it is difficult to identify how much investment underperformance was due to the referendum. https://obr.uk/box/g7-growth-investment-since-eu-referendum/
4. China, 2020: Growth slowed from \(6.1\%\) in 2019 to \(2.3\%\) in 2020, but remained positive. China’s National Bureau of Statistics also reported \(2.3\%\) growth for 2020. https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202101/t20210118_1812432.html



Real-World Application: Residential Construction vs. Existing Home Sales
When a family buys a newly built house, the value of the newly produced residential structure counts as residential investment in GDP. When another family buys an existing house, the sale price of the previously produced structure is an asset transfer, not current production. Current services connected to that sale, such as a real estate broker’s commission, do count because they are produced in the current period. The distinction is between the old asset and the new service, not between whether money changed hands.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
At each production stage \(i\), Value Added equals firm revenue minus intermediate input purchases:
\[
\text{Value Added}_i = \text{Sales Revenue}_i - \text{Cost of Intermediate Goods}_i, \qquad \text{GDP} = \sum_{i} \text{Value Added}_i
\]
Worked Problem: In this hypothetical 2026 accounting exercise, assume the domestic steel is used to make the new SUVs. Evaluate which transactions count in GDP and compute their combined contribution:

A U.S. automaker buys \(\$40\text{ million}\) of domestic steel to build new electric SUVs, which it sells to retail consumers for \(\$180\text{ million}\).
A retiree receives \(\$24{,}000\) in Social Security benefit payments.
A household buys a used 2022 sedan from a private seller for \(\$19{,}000\).
A state government spends \(\$65\text{ million}\) repaving interstate highways.

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Steel and New SUVs: The \(\$40\text{M}\) steel is an intermediate good already embedded in the final SUVs; count only the final retail value of \(\$180\text{ million}\) (\(\$40\text{M}\) steel value added plus \(\$140\text{M}\) automaker value added).
Social Security Payment: A government transfer payment redistributes income without purchasing current production (\(\$0\)).
Used 2022 Sedan: Secondhand asset transfer produced in an earlier year (\(\$0\)).
Highway Repaving: Current government purchases include the \(\$65\text{ million}\) spent on interstate repaving.

Conclusion: Total 2026 GDP contribution equals \(\$180\text{M} + \$0 + \$0 + \$65\text{M} = \mathbf{\$245\text{ million}}\).

title: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP
section: 4.2 Three Equivalent Approaches to Measuring GDP
text:
4.2 Three Equivalent Approaches to Measuring GDP

Conceptual Introduction
Because every dollar a buyer spends on a final good becomes a dollar of income for the workers, landlords, lenders, and business owners who produced it, national income accountants measure GDP using three equivalent perspectives:

The Expenditure Approach (\(Y = C + I + G + NX\)): Sums final spending across four sectors: Personal Consumption Expenditures (\(C\)), Gross Private Domestic Investment (\(I\)) (new business equipment, new residential housing, and changes in business inventories), Government Purchases (\(G\)) (excluding transfers), and Net Exports (\(NX = X - M\)). Imports (\(M\)) are subtracted because imported goods were already counted inside \(C\), \(I\), or \(G\) even though they were produced abroad.
The Income Approach (Gross Domestic Income, \(GDI\)): Sums all factor incomes earned in domestic production—wages and salaries, proprietors’ income, rental income, corporate profits, and net interest—plus indirect business taxes (less subsidies) and depreciation (consumption of fixed capital).
The Production (Value-Added) Approach: Sums value added across every industry sector.

These are three accounting views of the same production, not three different kinds of GDP to add together. In the expenditure view, the final buyer’s spending is counted once. In the production view, the same final value is built up as value added at each stage. In the income view, the revenues generated by production appear as income to workers, owners, lenders, and government. In principle, the totals are equal; in practice, GDP and gross domestic income are estimated from different data and can differ.


Visual Representation
Figure 3 is a schematic comparison, not a chart of measured component shares. It places the three accounting approaches side by side and emphasizes that each is intended to measure the same underlying domestic production.






NoteClear It Up: Why Are Imports Subtracted in \(Y = C + I + G + X - M\)?



Subtracting imports (\(-M\)) does not mean imports hurt GDP! When a U.S. consumer buys a \(\$1{,}000\) smartphone imported from abroad, Consumption (\(C\)) rises by \(+\$1{,}000\) and Imports (\(M\)) rise by \(+\$1{,}000\), so net U.S. GDP changes by \(\$1{,}000 - \$1{,}000 = \$0\)—accurately reflecting that the phone was produced outside U.S. borders.





Figure 3. Three Accounting Views of GDP. The expenditure, production, and income approaches are different ways to organize the value of current domestic production; the diagram is schematic and not proportional to observed shares.




Real-World Application: BEA Data Releases and FRED GDP and GDPC1 Data
The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) publishes quarterly national accounts tracked by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis’s FRED database. The GDP series (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDP) reports gross domestic product in billions of current dollars at a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR). The GDPC1 series (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPC1) reports real GDP in billions of chained 2017 dollars at a SAAR. A SAAR expresses the quarter’s pace as if it continued for a full year; it is not a separate observation of four quarters’ production.
GDP and GDI are compiled from different source data. Their difference is recorded as the statistical discrepancy; it is a measurement difference, not an additional type of production. Both series are revised as BEA incorporates new or updated data, so a reported historical value can change.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
The expenditure identity and Net Domestic Product (\(NDP\)) relations are:
\[
GDP = C + I + G + (X - M), \qquad NDP = GDP - \text{Depreciation}
\]
Worked Problem: Given the following national accounts data (in billions of dollars): Personal Consumption \(C = \$14{,}500\), Gross Private Domestic Investment \(I = \$3{,}800\), Government Purchases \(G = \$3{,}600\), Exports \(X = \$2{,}500\), Imports \(M = \$3{,}200\), and Depreciation \(= \$2{,}900\). Compute Net Exports (\(NX\)), Gross Domestic Product (\(GDP\)), and Net Domestic Product (\(NDP\)).
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute Net Exports (\(NX = X - M\)):

\[
NX = \$2{,}500 - \$3{,}200 = \mathbf{-\$700\text{ billion}}
\]

Compute Gross Domestic Product (\(GDP = C + I + G + NX\)):

\[
GDP = \$14{,}500 + \$3{,}800 + \$3{,}600 + (-\$700) = \mathbf{\$21{,}200\text{ billion}}
\]

Compute Net Domestic Product (\(NDP = GDP - \text{Depreciation}\)):

\[
NDP = \$21{,}200 - \$2{,}900 = \mathbf{\$18{,}300\text{ billion}}
\]
Conclusion: GDP is \(\$21{,}200\) billion and NDP is \(\$18{,}300\) billion.

title: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP
section: 4.3 Nominal GDP, Real GDP, and the GDP Deflator
text:
4.3 Nominal GDP, Real GDP, and the GDP Deflator

Conceptual Introduction
Suppose an economy’s dollar GDP increases by \(8\%\) this year. Did the economy produce more cars, haircuts, and software, or did prices rise while physical production stayed flat? Nominal GDP alone cannot separate those possibilities. To make the distinction, macroeconomists use two measures:

Nominal GDP: Values current-period production using current-period prices (\(\sum P_t Q_t\)). It can rise because quantities rise, prices rise, or both.
Real GDP: Adjusts the value of production to remove price change so that changes over time more closely track changes in output. In a simple fixed-base classroom example, this is calculated with base-year prices (\(\sum P_{\text{base}}Q_t\)). BEA’s official real GDP uses a chain-type quantity index, which updates price weights over time.

The ratio of nominal to real GDP, multiplied by 100, is the GDP implicit price deflator. It summarizes price changes for domestically produced final output. It differs from the Consumer Price Index (CPI): the GDP deflator covers domestic production, including investment and government output, while the CPI tracks a consumer basket that can include imported goods. Neither index is a cost-of-living measure for every household.


Visual Representation
Figure 4 is a schematic example. In the base year, nominal and real GDP are equal by construction; in later years, their gap reflects price changes as well as output changes. The lines are illustrative, not historical data.



Figure 4. Nominal GDP vs. Real GDP. In the base year, Nominal GDP and Real GDP are identical. When output and prices both rise after the base year, nominal GDP grows faster than real GDP because it reflects both changes.




Real-World Application: Reading GDP Alongside Other Indicators
Real GDP per capita is a commonly used indicator of average material output per person, but it is not a complete measure of living standards or welfare. It does not show how income is distributed and it does not directly measure unpaid care work, leisure, health, or environmental quality. Economists therefore use GDP alongside other indicators when a question concerns household well-being rather than production alone.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Nominal GDP, Real GDP, and the GDP Deflator satisfy:
\[
\text{GDP Deflator}_t = \frac{\text{Nominal GDP}_t}{\text{Real GDP}_t} \times 100
\]
Worked Problem: For a fixed-base instructional calculation, suppose an economy produces only two final goods: laptops and bicycles. In the 2024 base year, it produces \(100\) laptops at \(\$800\) each and \(200\) bicycles at \(\$300\) each. In 2026, it produces \(120\) laptops at \(\$900\) each and \(250\) bicycles at \(\$360\) each. Compute nominal GDP, real GDP at 2024 prices, and the GDP deflator for both years, plus real GDP growth.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute 2024 Base Year Values:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Nominal GDP}_{2024} = \text{Real GDP}_{2024}
&= (100 \times \$800) + (200 \times \$300) \\
&= \$80{,}000 + \$60{,}000 \\
&= \mathbf{\$140{,}000}
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\text{GDP Deflator}_{2024} = \frac{\$140{,}000}{\$140{,}000} \times 100 = \mathbf{100.0}
\]

Compute 2026 Nominal GDP (Using 2026 Prices):

\[
\text{Nominal GDP}_{2026} = (120 \times \$900) + (250 \times \$360) = \$108{,}000 + \$90{,}000 = \mathbf{\$198{,}000}
\]

Compute 2026 Real GDP (Using 2024 Base Prices):

\[
\text{Real GDP}_{2026} = (120 \times \$800) + (250 \times \$300) = \$96{,}000 + \$75{,}000 = \mathbf{\$171{,}000}
\]

Compute 2026 GDP Deflator and Real Output Growth:

\[
\text{GDP Deflator}_{2026} = \frac{\$198{,}000}{\$171{,}000} \times 100 \approx \mathbf{115.79}
\]
\[
\text{Real GDP Growth} = \frac{\$171{,}000 - \$140{,}000}{\$140{,}000} \times 100\% = \frac{\$31{,}000}{\$140{,}000} \times 100\% \approx \mathbf{+22.14\%}
\]
Conclusion: While Nominal GDP surged by \(41.43\%\), physical Real GDP grew by \(22.14\%\) and the overall GDP price level rose by \(15.79\%\).






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Chain-Weighted Real GDP Indices



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: With a fixed base year, the relative importance of goods can become outdated as prices and production patterns change. A Fisher quantity index balances a Laspeyres index, which values quantities using previous-period prices, and a Paasche index, which uses current-period prices. The geometric mean gives the two price-weighting perspectives equal influence:
\[
Q_t^{L} = \frac{\sum_i P_{i,t-1}Q_{i,t}}{\sum_i P_{i,t-1}Q_{i,t-1}}, \qquad
Q_t^{P} = \frac{\sum_i P_{i,t}Q_{i,t}}{\sum_i P_{i,t}Q_{i,t-1}}
\]
The chain-type quantity growth factor is:
\[
Q_t^{F} = \sqrt{Q_t^{L}Q_t^{P}}
\]
This extension explains why official chained-dollar component levels are generally not additive: the chain-type index is designed to measure growth across periods, not to preserve fixed-base component sums.

section: Practice and Self-Check
text:
Practice and Self-Check
Use the explanations after each answer to check both the correct reasoning and common distractors.

A domestic bakery buys \(\$2{,}000\) of flour and sells the bread made from it to households for \(\$5{,}000\). Ignoring other inputs, how much does the bread production contribute to GDP? (A) \(\$2{,}000\), (B) \(\$5{,}000\), or (C) \(\$7{,}000\).\ Answer: B. Count the final bread value once. A counts only the intermediate input; C adds the flour value again even though it is already embodied in the bread.
A U.S. household directly imports a newly produced \(\$1{,}000\) tablet from a foreign producer. What is the direct effect on U.S. GDP from the purchase? (A) It rises by \(\$1{,}000\), (B) it falls by \(\$1{,}000\), or (C) there is no direct change.\ Answer: C. Consumption rises by \(\$1{,}000\), but imports also rise by \(\$1{,}000\) and are subtracted in net exports. A ignores the foreign origin of production; B incorrectly treats the import adjustment as a loss of domestic output.
Nominal GDP rises while real GDP is unchanged. What happens to the GDP deflator? (A) It rises, (B) it falls, or (C) it stays unchanged.\ Answer: A. With real GDP fixed, a higher nominal value raises the nominal-to-real ratio. B reverses the ratio’s implication; C would require nominal GDP to stay fixed as well.
A household buys a newly built home and later buys an existing home from another household. Which transaction adds the structure’s value to current GDP?\ Answer: The newly built home adds current residential construction to investment. The existing structure was counted when it was produced; current brokerage services associated with its resale are counted separately.







NoteBring It Home: What GDP Can and Cannot Tell Us



GDP provides a consistent way to track the market value of current domestic production. To interpret a change, separate price movements from real output movements, check which production is domestic and current, and remember that a production total does not describe distribution or every dimension of well-being.

title: 5  Chapter 5: Unemployment and Inflation
text:
5.1 Learning Outcomes and Key Terms
By the end of this chapter, students should be able to classify people in the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) household-survey framework; calculate labor-force participation, employment-population, U-3, and U-6 rates; interpret unemployment and vacancy movements over the business cycle; estimate an illustrative output loss with Okun’s law; and distinguish nominal wage growth from changes in real purchasing power. Key terms include civilian noninstitutional population, labor force, not in the labor force, marginally attached, underemployment, U-3, U-6, Beveridge curve, potential output, CPI, and real wage.

title: 5  Chapter 5: Unemployment and Inflation
section: 5.2 Part 1: The BLS Population Map
text:
5.2 Part 1: The BLS Population Map

5.2.1 Bring It Home: One Person, One Survey Week
Imagine that a worker’s restaurant closes for renovations during the BLS survey reference week. The worker did no paid work that week, is available, is on temporary layoff, and expects to be recalled within six months; the worker has not searched elsewhere. Another person worked a paid shift for a delivery platform, even though the work was only a few hours. A third person wants a job but stopped searching after repeated rejections. These people may all describe themselves as needing more work, but the household survey classifies them differently using consistent rules.
The starting population is the civilian noninstitutional population (CNIP) age 16 and older, denoted \(P\). The BLS partitions it into people in the labor force and people not in the labor force:
\[
P = LF + NILF, \qquad LF = E + U.
\]
Here \(E\) is employed, \(U\) is unemployed, \(LF\) is the labor force, and \(NILF\) is not in the labor force. A person is employed if they did work for pay or profit during the reference week, worked without pay for at least 15 hours in a family-owned business or farm, or had a job but were temporarily absent. A person is generally unemployed if they had no job, were available for work, and actively searched in the prior four weeks. A person on temporary layoff can be counted as unemployed without searching if they have been given a return date or expect to return within six months. Everyone else in \(P\) is classified as not in the labor force.






NoteSSOT Benchmark: Population and Headline Rates



For the Master Summary benchmark, \(P=200\) million, \(LF=120\) million, \(E=114\) million, and \(U=6\) million. Thus \(U\)-\(3=6/120\times100\%=5.0\%\) and \(LFPR=120/200\times100\%=60.0\%\). A U-6 calculation also requires counts for marginally attached people and employed part-time workers for economic reasons; those component counts are not specified here.




5.2.2 Graph Description: The BLS Classification Tree
Picture a flowchart rather than a graph with a behavioral curve. At the top is the full rectangle \(P\). A vertical split separates \(LF\) on the left from \(NILF\) on the right. The \(LF\) rectangle splits again into \(E\) and \(U\). Every person belongs to exactly one leaf of this tree for the survey classification. The categories describe survey status, not a person’s worth, effort, or need for income.



Figure 1. The BLS population partition. Each person in the civilian noninstitutional population is classified as employed, unemployed, or not in the labor force; employed and unemployed people together make up the labor force.




5.2.3 Work It Out: Rates Have Different Denominators
Suppose a hypothetical local population has \(P=1{,}000\), with \(E=600\), \(U=40\), and therefore \(NILF=360\). First add employed and unemployed people to find the labor force: \[\begin{align}
LF &= E+U = 600+40=640,\\
u_3 &= \frac{U}{LF}\times 100\% = \frac{40}{640}\times100\%=6.25\%,\\
LFPR &= \frac{LF}{P}\times100\% = \frac{640}{1{,}000}\times100\%=64\%,\\
EPOP &= \frac{E}{P}\times100\% = \frac{600}{1{,}000}\times100\%=60\%.
\end{align}\] The unemployment rate is not the share of the entire population without a job. Its denominator is the labor force. The participation rate asks what share of the population is working or actively seeking work; the employment-population ratio asks what share is employed.






NoteClear It Up: A Falling U-3 Rate Can Hide a Falling Labor Force



If unemployed people stop searching, they generally move from \(U\) to \(NILF\). That lowers both the numerator and denominator of U-3 and can make the rate fall without any new hiring. Check \(LFPR\) and \(EPOP\) alongside unemployment before concluding that job conditions improved.

title: 5  Chapter 5: Unemployment and Inflation
section: 5.3 Part 2: U-3, U-6, and the Gig Economy
text:
5.3 Part 2: U-3, U-6, and the Gig Economy

5.3.1 The Headline Rate and Broader Underutilization
U-3 is the official unemployment rate: unemployed people as a share of the civilian labor force. It is useful, comparable, and deliberately narrow. It does not count people who want a job but have not searched recently, and it counts a person working part time as employed even if that person wants full-time hours.
U-6 is a broader BLS measure of labor underutilization. It includes the unemployed, people marginally attached to the labor force, and people employed part time for economic reasons. The latter category includes people working fewer than 35 hours for an economic reason who want and are available for full-time work. Marginally attached people want and are available for work, searched sometime in the prior 12 months, but did not search during the most recent four weeks. Discouraged workers are one subset of the marginally attached. U-6’s denominator adds the marginally attached to the labor force, so the numerator and denominator must be expanded together:
\[
U\text{-}6 =
\frac{U + M + PT_{econ}}{LF + M}\times100\%,
\]
where \(M\) is marginally attached people and \(PT_{econ}\) is employed part-time for economic reasons.


5.3.2 Bring It Home: A Platform Worker Wants More Hours
A courier completes several paid deliveries during the reference week and wants a stable, full-time schedule. Under the household-survey concept, the courier is employed because they performed paid work; being a gig worker does not by itself make someone unemployed. If the courier works fewer than 35 hours for an economic reason and wants and is available for full-time hours, they may be included in the U-6 numerator but not in U-3’s unemployed count. Another courier who did no work, wants a job, is available, and searched within the last four weeks may be unemployed. A worker who stopped searching may be marginally attached, rather than unemployed under U-3.
The distinction is about measured labor utilization, not whether a gig job is good or bad. The survey classification alone does not reveal earnings volatility, benefits, schedule control, job security, or whether the worker prefers independent contracting. Those are important dimensions of job quality, but they require additional data.


5.3.3 Work It Out: Compare U-3 and U-6
Continue the hypothetical example with \(LF=640\) and \(U=40\). Suppose \(M=20\) people are marginally attached and \(PT_{econ}=30\) employed people want full-time work but can only find part-time hours. Then: \[\begin{align}
U\text{-}3 &= \frac{40}{640}\times100\%=6.25\%,\\
U\text{-}6 &= \frac{40+20+30}{640+20}\times100\%
=\frac{90}{660}\times100\%\approx13.64\%.
\end{align}\] These are illustrative counts, not a current estimate for any city or month. The gap between the measures shows that the headline rate omits forms of underutilization; it does not mean U-3 is incorrectly calculated.



Figure 2. Illustrative U-3 and U-6 rates from the hypothetical counts in this section. The measures use different definitions and denominators; these values are not current estimates.








TipFRED Data: Compare Measures, Not Just Headlines



FRED distributes official BLS series including UNRATE (U-3), U6RATE (U-6), CIVPART (labor-force participation rate), and EMRATIO (employment-population ratio). These are seasonally adjusted monthly percentage series. Plotting them together can show whether a change in U-3 coincides with movement in broader underutilization or participation. The rates have different definitions and denominators; their difference is informative, not an arithmetic error.

title: 5  Chapter 5: Unemployment and Inflation
section: 5.4 Part 3: Vacancies, Unemployment, and Output Slack
text:
5.4 Part 3: Vacancies, Unemployment, and Output Slack

5.4.1 The Beveridge Curve
The Beveridge curve describes the usual inverse relationship between the unemployment rate and the job-vacancy rate. In a Cartesian diagram, place unemployment \(u\) (percent) on the horizontal axis and vacancies \(v\) (percent) on the vertical axis. Along a given curve, an up-left movement means vacancies rise while unemployment falls; a down-right movement means vacancies fall while unemployment rises. These movements can reflect changes in labor demand. This is a descriptive relationship, not a mechanical law.
The curve can shift. Improved matching, geographic mobility, or training can move the relationship inward, allowing more hires for a given vacancy rate. Mismatch between workers’ skills and open jobs, search frictions, or slower matching can shift it outward. A point on the curve is an observed combination; a shift is a change in the relationship itself.



Figure 3. A downward-sloping Beveridge relationship and an outward shift associated with weaker matching. Curves and endpoints are shown within the labeled 0–10 percent plotting range.




5.4.2 Okun’s Law: From an Unemployment Gap to an Output Gap
Okun’s law summarizes a regularity: when unemployment is above its sustainable or natural benchmark, real output tends to be below potential. The relationship helps policymakers interpret labor-market slack alongside production, but it is an empirical approximation rather than a causal law. A simplified gap form is:
\[
\frac{Y-Y^*}{Y^*}\times100\%\approx -\beta(u_{\rm pp}-u^*_{\rm pp}), \qquad \beta>0,
\]
where \(Y\) is real output, \(Y^*\) is potential output, and \(u_{\rm pp}\) and \(u^*_{\rm pp}\) are unemployment rates stated in percentage-point units. The coefficient \(\beta\) is the percentage-point output gap associated with a one-percentage-point unemployment gap; it varies by period and specification.



Figure 4. Illustrative Okun relationship when \(\beta=2\): a two-percentage-point unemployment gap corresponds to an estimated output gap of \(-4\%\). The line is a schematic, not an estimated time series.


Application: A local policymaker comparing employment conditions across neighborhoods might use unemployment and output-gap estimates together when assessing a downturn. Neither measure alone identifies the cause of the decline, and both the potential-output benchmark and Okun coefficient must be stated.


5.4.3 Work It Out: An Illustrative $1.0 Trillion Output Shortfall
Assume potential real GDP is \(Y^*=\$25.0\) trillion in a chosen base-year dollar measure, actual unemployment is \(u_{\rm pp}=6\), the estimated benchmark is \(u^*_{\rm pp}=4\), and an illustrative Okun coefficient is \(\beta=2\). First find the unemployment gap: \(6-4=2\) percentage points. Then estimate the output gap: \[\begin{align}
\frac{Y-Y^*}{Y^*}\times100\% &\approx -2(6-4)=-4\%,\\
Y^*-Y &\approx 0.04\times \$25.0\text{ trillion}
=\$1.0\text{ trillion}.
\end{align}\] The estimated shortfall is $1.0 trillion of real output relative to the assumed potential level. This is a model-based illustration, not a reported current loss. Potential GDP and \(\beta\) are estimates, and the result depends on the units and period used.






NoteOptional Advanced: Markov Job-Finding and Separation Flows



In a two-state model, let \(s\) be the period separation probability from employment to unemployment and \(f\) the job-finding probability from unemployment to employment. At steady state, inflows to unemployment equal outflows: \(s(1-u)=fu\). Solving gives:
\[
u^*=\frac{s}{s+f}.
\]
This result assumes a stable two-state population, constant transition probabilities, and no labor-force entry or exit. It makes the stock-flow logic explicit: a higher separation rate raises steady-state unemployment, while a higher job-finding rate lowers it.








NoteOptional Advanced: State-Space Slack and Growth-Rate Okun Relations



Potential output \(Y_t^*\) and the natural unemployment rate \(u_t^*\) are not directly observed. A state-space approach treats them as latent states inferred from noisy observations. Output slack can be represented as \(x_t=\ln Y_t-\ln Y_t^*\), approximately the percentage output gap for small differences; labor slack can be represented as \(u_t-u_t^*\). Their estimated paths depend on the model and can be revised as new observations arrive.
An alternative growth-difference form is \(\Delta u_t\approx-\kappa(g_{Y,t}-g_{Y,t}^*)\), where \(g_{Y,t}\) is real output growth, \(g_{Y,t}^*\) is potential growth, and \(\kappa>0\) is an estimated response coefficient. Growth above potential tends to reduce unemployment; growth below potential tends to raise it. This is an empirical approximation, not an identity.

title: 5  Chapter 5: Unemployment and Inflation
section: 5.5 Part 4: CPI Inflation and Real-Wage Purchasing Power
text:
5.5 Part 4: CPI Inflation and Real-Wage Purchasing Power

5.5.1 A Price Index and the Cost of a Basket
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks price changes for a representative consumer basket under the BLS methodology. Inflation over a period is the percentage change in the index:
\[
\pi_t=\frac{CPI_t-CPI_{t-1}}{CPI_{t-1}}\times100\%.
\]
The CPI is an index, not a dollar price and not a perfect measure of every household’s cost of living. Households have different spending patterns, and the index summarizes an average basket using a defined method.


5.5.2 Nominal Wages and Real Purchasing Power
A nominal wage is measured in current dollars. A real wage adjusts for the price level and indicates how much of a reference-period basket that wage can buy:
\[
W^{real,0}_t=W^{nom}_t\frac{CPI_0}{CPI_t},
\]
where \(CPI_0\) is the CPI in the chosen base period. If the CPI series is not rebased to that period, use the ratio \(CPI_0/CPI_t\). When nominal wages rise more slowly than prices, purchasing power falls even though the dollar wage increased.
Application: When workers and employers discuss an annual raise, comparing nominal wage growth with inflation helps distinguish a larger paycheck from a gain in purchasing power. The numerical values below are illustrative, not a current wage or CPI observation.


5.5.3 Work It Out: A Raise That Does Not Keep Pace with Prices
Suppose an hourly wage rises from $20.00 to $20.80, a 4% increase. Over the same period, the CPI rises from 300 to 315, a 5% increase. Express the new wage in the initial period’s purchasing power: \[\begin{align}
W^{real,0}_0 &= \$20.00\frac{300}{300}=\$20.00,\\
W^{real,0}_1 &= \$20.80\frac{300}{315}\approx \$19.81.
\end{align}\] The real wage changes by approximately \((19.81/20.00)-1=-0.95\%\). The worker receives 80 cents more per hour in nominal terms, but the CPI basket costs more, so purchasing power falls slightly.



Figure 5. Illustrative index changes from period 0 to period 1. With nominal wages indexed to 100 initially, the wage index rises 4 points while CPI rises 5 points, so the real-wage index falls to about 99.05.








NoteClear It Up: Nominal Raise Does Not Guarantee a Real Raise



Compare growth rates, not dollar changes alone. When nominal wage growth is below inflation, real wage growth is negative. When the two rates are close, the approximation \(g_{real}\approx g_W-\pi\) is useful, but exact compounding gives a slightly different result.








NoteOptional Advanced: Exact Real-Wage Growth Identity



The exact relation between nominal wage growth \(g_W\), inflation \(\pi\), and real wage growth \(g_{real}\) is:
\[
1+g_{real}=\frac{1+g_W}{1+\pi},
\qquad
g_{real}=\frac{1+g_W}{1+\pi}-1.
\]
For \(g_W=0.04\) and \(\pi=0.05\), exact real growth is \(1.04/1.05-1\approx-0.00952\), or about \(-0.95\%\). The subtraction approximation gives \(4\%-5\%=-1\%\). The difference is small here but matters when rates are large.








TipFRED Data: Track Inflation and Real-Wage Context



FRED series CPIAUCSL is the seasonally adjusted U.S. all-items CPI for all urban consumers, reported monthly as an index with 1982–84=100. UNRATE and U6RATE report U-3 and U-6, while CIVPART and EMRATIO provide participation and employment-population context. To study purchasing power, compare nominal wage growth with CPI inflation over matching dates and frequencies; do not divide a wage by an index without stating the chosen base convention.

title: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
text:
6.1 Learning Outcomes and Key Terms
Students should distinguish saving from wealth, apply the national saving identity, and use the loanable-funds model to explain how saving and investment plans respond to real interest rates. These objectives support MA-2 and MA-3 and prepare students for C2002-2. Key terms include private saving, public saving, national saving, investment, loanable funds, real interest rate, deficit, and capital inflow.
crumbs: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System

title: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
section: 6.2 Saving Is a Flow; Wealth Is a Stock
text:
6.2 Saving Is a Flow; Wealth Is a Stock
A household that saves part of this month’s income adds to its assets, but saving itself is measured over a period. Wealth is the value of assets held at a point in time. Likewise, investment in macroeconomics is spending on newly produced capital goods and inventories during a period; it is not the purchase of an existing stock certificate. Keeping stocks and flows separate prevents a common accounting error.
crumbs: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System

title: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
section: 6.3 National Saving and the Open-Economy Identity
text:
6.3 National Saving and the Open-Economy Identity
Start with the expenditure identity \(Y=C+I+G+NX\). Rearranging gives \(Y-C-G=I+NX\). National saving is \(S=Y-C-G\), so in the simplified model \(S=I+NX\). If net exports are used as the current-account proxy, then \(S-I=NX\): saving above domestic investment corresponds to net lending abroad, while investment above saving is matched by net borrowing from abroad. In full balance-of-payments accounts, the current account includes net primary income and transfers as well as goods and services.
With taxes \(T\) and disposable income \(Y-T\), private saving is \(S_p=Y-T-C\) and public saving is \(S_g=T-G\). National saving adds the two: \[\begin{equation}
S=S_p+S_g=(Y-T-C)+(T-G)=Y-C-G, \qquad S-I=NX \quad\text{(simplified model)}.
\end{equation}\] In a closed economy, \(NX=0\) and planned national saving equals investment in the accounting identity. The identity does not guarantee that desired saving and planned investment are equal at every interest rate; prices, output, and financial markets adjust toward consistency.
crumbs: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System

title: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
section: 6.4 Loanable Funds: Graph and Mechanism
text:
6.4 Loanable Funds: Graph and Mechanism
Put the quantity of loanable funds on the horizontal axis and the real interest rate on the vertical axis. Planned saving is drawn as a supply of funds, often rising with the real return. Planned investment is a demand for funds, often falling as borrowing becomes more expensive. Their intersection is the model’s equilibrium real rate and quantity. A shift in saving or investment plans moves one curve; a change in the interest rate is a movement along a curve. This is a market model, not a literal inventory of all bank deposits.
crumbs: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System

title: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
section: 6.5 Deficits, Interest Rates, and Crowding Out
text:
6.5 Deficits, Interest Rates, and Crowding Out
If government purchases rise while taxes and private saving behavior are fixed, public saving falls. In a closed-economy loanable-funds model, the saving supply can shift left, raising the equilibrium real interest rate and reducing some private investment. This is the crowding-out mechanism. Its size depends on conditions: monetary policy, spare capacity, household saving responses, international capital flows, and the central bank’s reaction can change the outcome. A deficit does not mechanically imply a one-for-one decline in private investment.






TipFRED Data: Gross Private Domestic Investment



FRED series GPDI reports gross private domestic investment in billions of current dollars at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, quarterly. It includes fixed investment and inventory change. It is a nominal expenditure flow, not a capital stock and not a direct measure of productive capacity. To study physical investment growth across time, compare an appropriate real series and account for revisions and price changes.








NoteClear It Up: The Identity Is Not a Causal Claim



The accounting relation \(S-I=NX\) in the simplified model must hold ex post. It does not by itself tell us whether saving caused investment, investment caused income and saving, or foreign flows adjusted. Use a behavioral model and evidence to discuss causation.
crumbs: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System

title: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
section: 6.6 Check Your Understanding
text:
6.6 Check Your Understanding

If \(Y=1{,}000\), \(C=650\), and \(G=200\), calculate national saving.
If national saving is 150 and investment is 180, what is \(NX\) in the simplified open-economy identity?
Is buying an existing share of a company macroeconomic investment? Why or why not?

Answers: (1) \(S=Y-C-G=150\). (2) \(NX=S-I=-30\), a deficit in the simplified model. (3) No; it transfers ownership of an existing financial asset rather than purchasing newly produced capital.
